teaser: Painted for a hospital where the dying were carried in to look at it.
review_notes:
The photo shows the altarpiece in its closed (first) view as installed at the Unterlinden Museum: Crucifixion, Saint Sebastian (left), Saint Anthony (right), Lamentation predella. The lesson only points at this view.
Listed year 1515; the work is usually dated about 1512 to 1516.
Crucifixion panel about 2.7 x 3.1 m.
Ergotism (Saint Anthony's fire) caused by ergot fungus on rye; the Antonite hospital at Isenheim; new patients brought before the altarpiece: standard account, please verify wording.
The reading of the off-center seam (Christ's arm separated when the panels open) as an echo of amputations is an interpretation, presented as such.
Grünewald's real name Mathis Gothart Nithart; 'Grünewald' introduced by Joachim von Sandrart in 1675.
Sculpted shrine by Nikolaus of Haguenau.
Altarpiece moved to Colmar during the French Revolution; taken to Munich in the First World War and returned in 1919.
Hindemith's opera 'Mathis der Maler' (1930s); influence on Otto Dix and Picasso (1932 drawings).
Latin inscription by John the Baptist: 'Illum oportet crescere, me autem minui'. It is barely legible in this photo.
The demon at Saint Anthony's window is small in this photo.

lesson.text: The head has just dropped. A second ago this man was still pulling air into his chest, and the fingers have not understood yet: they are still spread wide, clawing at a black sky. A woman in white is halfway through fainting. That is the instant this painting holds, the first moment after the last breath.

The painter is known as Matthias Grünewald, and he worked on it for several years around 1515. The central panel is huge, about 2.7 m high and 3 m wide (roughly 9 by 10 feet), so the body hangs above you at more than life size. Before any history, see how much is still moving.

lesson.title: One second after
lesson.text: Four places where the picture catches a movement that has not finished.

spots.title: The fingers
spots.text: The nailed hand is not limp. Each finger stiffens upward in a different direction, like a cramp. The crossbeam itself bends downward at both ends under the weight.

spots.title: The fallen head
spots.text: The chin has sunk onto the chest and the mouth hangs open. The crown is a thicket of long thorns, far bigger than the neat circle most painters gave it.

spots.title: The faint
spots.text: Mary, in white like a nun or a shroud, tips backward with her eyes closed and her hands still clasped. John the Evangelist, in red, catches her. Her body makes a pale curve.

spots.title: The wrung hands
spots.text: Mary Magdalene kneels, small as a child next to the cross, her head thrown back. Her fingers are locked together and twisted upward. They answer the fingers on the cross above.

lesson.text: Now the skin. This body is greenish, and it is covered from shoulders to shins in small dark sores and splinters. No Italian painter of the time would have shown Christ like this. Grünewald had a reason, and the reason was his audience.

The altarpiece was made for the church of a hospital at Isenheim, a village in Alsace, in what is now eastern France. The monks who ran it, the order of Saint Anthony, took in people with a disease called Saint Anthony's fire. It burned in the limbs, covered the skin in sores and turned hands and feet black.

Nobody then knew the cause. Saint Anthony's fire is poisoning by ergot, a fungus that grows on rye in wet years and ends up in the bread. It strangles the blood supply, which is why victims felt they were burning and often lost fingers, feet or whole limbs.

New patients were brought in front of this painting as part of their care. What they saw was not a calm, beautiful god. They saw their own skin on him. The message did not need a sermon: he has what you have, and he is with you in it.
The horror here is a form of kindness. Grünewald painted Christ's body to look like the bodies of the people who would be praying to it.

On the right stands a man who should not be here. John the Baptist had been beheaded well before the Crucifixion. Grünewald brings him back anyway, calm, feet planted, a book open in one hand. He is not part of the instant. He is there to explain it.
The whole panel is organized by a few directions. Follow them.

lines.label: The finger
lines.text: John's arm bends at the elbow and ends in a huge forefinger, longer than any real one. Extend it and you land on Christ's chest. It is a painted arrow: look there.

lines.label: The V of the arms
lines.text: The arms are stretched so far that they form a shallow V, with the fallen head at its point. The body does not stand on the cross. It hangs from it with all its weight.

lines.label: The falling curve
lines.text: On the left, John the Evangelist's head, Mary's face and her long white robe form one arc bending away from the cross, like something being blown backward.

lines.label: The seam
lines.text: A thin vertical join runs just left of Christ's body. The panel is made of two doors, and they meet here. Remember this line.

lesson.text: Between John's finger and his face, red Latin words float on the dark: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” It is a line from the Gospels, spoken by the Baptist about Jesus. Sizes follow importance too. Christ is the giant of the scene and Magdalene the smallest, an old medieval habit Grünewald kept on purpose.

“Grünewald” is a mistake. A German writer gave him that name in 1675, some 150 years after his death, and it stuck. Documents suggest he was really called Mathis Gothart Nithart. Hardly anything is known about his life, and only a small number of his paintings survive.

The side panels bring in two bodyguards. On the left, Saint Sebastian, pierced by arrows, was prayed to against the plague. On the right, old Saint Anthony with his T-shaped staff was the patron of the hospital and of its disease. Both stand on stone bases like painted statues. Anthony's corner is less quiet than it looks.
Something is attacking the window behind one of the two saints on the wings. Which window, and what is it?

spots.title: The demon
spots.text: Behind Saint Anthony, at the top right, a dark horned creature presses against the round panes and breaks through the glass. Legends tell of demons tormenting Anthony. He does not turn around.

lesson.text: This is only the altarpiece's everyday face. It is a machine with doors. Open the Crucifixion and a second set of paintings appears, blazing with color: angels playing music, a birth, and Christ rising in a ball of light, his skin now clean. Open again and you reach gilded wooden statues carved by another artist, Nikolaus of Haguenau.

The doors part along the seam you saw, which is off-center. As they swing open, Christ's arm separates from his body. In the long panel underneath, which also slides apart, the join falls across his legs. Many historians think patients facing amputation were meant to notice.

spots.title: The lamb
spots.text: A white lamb holds a thin cross, and blood runs from its chest into a gold cup. It is a symbol of Christ as a sacrifice, and of the wine at Mass. It looks out calmly.

spots.title: The ointment jar
spots.text: A small lidded pot on the ground next to Magdalene. It is her usual attribute, the jar of perfumed oil with which she anointed Jesus.

spots.title: The feet
spots.text: One nail goes through both feet, which twist over each other. The toes are swollen and dark, close to what the hospital's patients saw at the end of their own legs.

spots.title: INRI
spots.text: The sign on top carries the Latin initials for “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews”, the charge posted on the cross.

spots.title: Saint Sebastian
spots.text: Arrows stick out of him and lie against the column, yet he stands relaxed, hands joined, in a red cloak. Through the window behind him, angels fly down with a crown.

spots.title: Saint Anthony
spots.text: A white-bearded hermit in a red cap and a rose cloak over dark robes, holding a staff topped with a T-shaped cross, the badge of the monks who ran the hospital.

spots.title: The body laid out
spots.text: In the low panel at the bottom, called a predella, the dead Christ is lowered toward an open stone tomb. The sores are still there. Mary, veiled in white, weeps behind him.

lesson.text: During the French Revolution the monastery was closed and the panels were carried to the nearby town of Colmar for safety. They are still there, in a former convent that became the Unterlinden Museum. In the First World War they were taken to Munich, and their return in 1919 was treated as a national event.

After centuries of neglect, the 20th century recognized itself in this painting. Artists who had seen the trenches, like the German Otto Dix, went back to it. Picasso drew his own versions of the Crucifixion from it in 1932. A composer, Paul Hindemith, wrote an entire opera about its maker. A picture built to comfort the sick of one village had found a much larger ward.

quiz.question: Who was the altarpiece painted for?
options: A hospital church whose patients had a skin and limb disease
quiz.explanation: It was made for the hospital of the order of Saint Anthony at Isenheim.

quiz.question: Why is Christ's skin covered in sores?
options: The paint has decayed over time
It was the usual way to paint him in Italy
So the sick could see their own suffering in him
quiz.explanation: Grünewald gave Christ a body like those of the hospital's patients.

quiz.question: What causes Saint Anthony's fire?
options: A fungus that grows on rye
quiz.explanation: It is poisoning by ergot, a fungus on rye that ends up in bread.

quiz.question: Why is John the Baptist's presence strange?
options: He was never a follower of Jesus
He had died before the Crucifixion
He is shown as a child
quiz.explanation: He had been beheaded earlier, so Grünewald brings him back to point and explain.

quiz.question: What is breaking through the window behind Saint Anthony?
quiz.explanation: A dark horned creature smashes the round panes behind the saint.

quiz.question: What happens when the two halves of the Crucifixion are opened?
quiz.explanation: The altarpiece has doors that reveal a second set of paintings, and then carved statues.

facts.text: The painter's real name was almost certainly not Grünewald.
facts.explanation: A writer gave him that name in 1675; documents point to Mathis Gothart Nithart.

facts.text: In the Crucifixion, Mary Magdalene is painted larger than Christ.
facts.explanation: She is the smallest figure and Christ the largest, following importance.

facts.text: The altarpiece is still in the hospital church at Isenheim.
facts.explanation: It was moved to Colmar during the French Revolution and is in the Unterlinden Museum.
